name: Causes of revolution and 'equality according to proportion'
plain_explanation: Aristotle argues that revolutions arise from the clash between democrats, who think that people equally free should be equal in everything, and oligarchs, who think that people superior in some respect deserve more of everything; he proposes preventing revolution through civic education, respect for law, and 'equality according to proportion' -- rewarding people in proportion to their merit.
precise_definition: Aristotle's analysis (drawing on extensive comparative experience of Greek civil conflict) that revolution is chiefly caused by the competing partial justices of democratic and oligarchic factions, to be forestalled by government-aligned education, habitual respect for law even in small matters, and proportional (merit-based) rather than strictly equal distribution of political goods.
why_it_mattered: Russell uses it to expose a deep practical difficulty in Aristotle's own theory: since virtue is hard to measure and contested, 'proportionate justice' collapses in practice into measuring worth by income, undermining Aristotle's attempted distinction between a genuine aristocracy (rule of the virtuous) and a mere oligarchy (rule of the rich).
historical_origin: Drawn from Aristotle's wide comparative knowledge of Greek civil conflict, which Russell compares to 'formerly in Latin America' in frequency.
examples: An oligarchic oath quoted by Aristotle: 'I will be an enemy to the people, and will devise all the harm against them which I can.'
objections: Russell: virtue is difficult to measure and is 'a matter of party controversy'; in practice, 'virtue tends to be measured by income,' so the distinction Aristotle wants between aristocracy and oligarchy 'is only possible where there is a very well-established hereditary nobility,' and even then breaks down once a large non-noble rich class arises and must be admitted to power to avert revolution.
competing_positions: Russell's own conclusion that 'all social inequality, in the long run, is inequality of income,' which he treats as part of the argument for democracy over any scheme of 'proportionate justice' based on supposedly measurable merit.
